topics.title: What are Database Isolation Levels and What are They Used For?
topics.overview: Database isolation levels define how changes made by one transaction (a unit of work) are visible to other concurrent (simultaneous) transactions. They manage the trade-off between strict data consistency and database performance.

key_term_definitions.transaction: A single logical unit of work (e.g., deducting money from Account A and adding it to Account B) that must either completely succeed or completely fail.
key_term_definitions.acid_properties: A set of properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) that guarantee database transactions are processed reliably.
key_term_definitions.concurrency: The ability of a system to execute multiple database read/write operations at the exact same time.

purpose: Prevent data anomalies like Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Phantom Reads.
Ensure reliable transaction processing without data corruption.
Allow system architects to tune database speed vs correctness.

concurrency_phenomena_explained.dirty_read: Transaction A modifies a row but hasn't saved it (commit). Transaction B reads this uncommitted row. Transaction A cancels (rollback). Transaction B now has fake/invalid data.
concurrency_phenomena_explained.non_repeatable_read: Transaction A reads a row. Transaction B updates that same row and saves. Transaction A reads it again and gets a different value.
concurrency_phenomena_explained.phantom_read: Transaction A queries a range of rows (e.g., users with age > 25). Transaction B inserts a new user with age 26. Transaction A re-runs the query and finds an extra 'phantom' row.

isolation_levels.mechanism: No locking or verification. Transactions read uncommitted data directly.
isolation_levels.real_tech_example: YouTube Video View Counter or Live Stream Viewer Count: It doesn't matter if the count is slightly off by 2-3 views due to uncommitted writes, as speed is prioritized over 100% precision.

isolation_levels.mechanism: Transactions can only read data that has been permanently saved (committed).
isolation_levels.real_tech_example: Social Media Feeds (Instagram/Twitter): You won't see a drafted or discarded post. Default setting in PostgreSQL and SQL Server.

isolation_levels.mechanism: Locks the rows involved in a read operation so no other transaction can modify them until the transaction finishes.
suffers_from: Phantom Read (prevented in MySQL InnoDB using Next-Key Locking)
isolation_levels.real_tech_example: E-commerce Inventory Stock Checkout (Amazon): When you add the last laptop to your cart, another buyer cannot change its stock status while your transaction is running.

isolation_levels.mechanism: Completely isolates transactions by running them sequentially (one after another).
isolation_levels.real_tech_example: Banking Core Account Transfer (HDFC/Chase) or Flight Seat Booking (BookMyShow/Airline): Ensures two people sitting on different sides of the world cannot buy the exact same seat at the same millisecond.

topics.title: What is IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS?
topics.overview: These three cloud computing service models dictate how much control you have over your hardware and software stack versus how much the cloud vendor manages for you.

key_term_definitions.cloud_vendor: A company (like AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure) that owns huge data centers and rents out computing power over the internet.
key_term_definitions.runtime: The environment (like Node.js, Python VM, JVM) that executes your written programming code.

iaas.explanation: You rent raw physical or virtual machines, storage, and networking. You install the OS, setup databases, and handle security patches yourself.
iaas.real_tech_example: Netflix hosting its custom video encoding infrastructure on AWS EC2 instances, giving them total control over OS-level performance tuning.

paas.explanation: The provider handles hardware, OS, and software runtimes. You simply upload your application code and config files.
paas.real_tech_example: A startup deploying a Node.js API to Heroku or AWS Elastic Beanstalk using `git push heroku main` without worrying about Ubuntu security patches or server setup.

saas.explanation: Fully built, web-accessible software. You just log in and use it.
provider_manages: Everything (Code, Hardware, Security, Scaling, Database, Upgrades)
saas.real_tech_example: Companies using Google Workspace (Gmail/Docs) or Figma for team design, where zero code or infrastructure setup is required.

topics.title: Most Popular Programming Languages & Their System Design Roles

key_term_definitions.microservices: An architectural style where an application is broken down into small, independent services that communicate over a network.
key_term_definitions.throughput: The amount of data or number of requests a system can process in a given amount of time.
key_term_definitions.latency: The time delay between a user making a request and receiving a response.

languages.name: Python
languages.strengths: Simple syntax, massive ecosystem of AI/ML libraries (PyTorch, TensorFlow, Pandas).
languages.system_design_role: Asynchronous background processing, Machine Learning inference pipelines, Data Analysis engines.
languages.real_tech_example: Instagram's primary backend API running on Django, and OpenAI using Python as the main wrapper language for its AI model endpoints.

languages.name: Java
languages.strengths: Runs on JVM (Java Virtual Machine), battle-tested stability, highly optimized garbage collection for large memory footprints.
languages.system_design_role: High-throughput enterprise backends, large distributed storage management.
languages.real_tech_example: Uber and LinkedIn's core backend platform services built on Java/Spring Boot handling millions of requests per minute.

languages.name: JavaScript / TypeScript
languages.strengths: Runs everywhere (Browser and Node.js Server), non-blocking event-driven I/O model.
languages.system_design_role: Client-side single-page apps (SPA), API Gateways, Real-time WebSocket servers.
languages.real_tech_example: Slack and Discord utilizing TypeScript for cross-platform desktop UI (Electron) and real-time chat messaging channels.

languages.name: Go (Golang)
languages.strengths: Lightweight concurrency via Goroutines, extremely fast execution speed, low memory usage.
languages.system_design_role: High-performance microservices, API Proxies, Networking infrastructure software.
languages.real_tech_example: Docker, Kubernetes, and Twitch chat server backends handling millions of concurrent video viewers using Goroutines.

languages.name: C++
languages.strengths: Direct memory allocation, zero overhead abstractions, ultra-low latency.
languages.system_design_role: Core infrastructure engines, high-frequency trading (HFT) platforms, database internal storage engines.
languages.real_tech_example: Google Search Indexing engine, MySQL/PostgreSQL core engines, and Chromium browser rendering pipeline.

topics.title: What is the Future of Online Payments?
topics.overview: Online payments are shifting away from traditional 3-day settlement credit card networks toward instant, low-fee, programmable, and cryptographic networks.

key_term_definitions.settlement_network: The behind-the-scenes system that actually moves money from one bank account to another.
key_term_definitions.interchange_fee: The fee (typically 1.5% - 3.5%) charged by card issuers (Visa/Mastercard) to merchants for processing payments.

key_trends.explanation: Bypassing Visa/Mastercard channels by directly transferring money from customer bank accounts to merchant bank accounts instantly using central bank APIs.
key_trends.real_tech_example: UPI in India (handling over 10 billion transactions monthly) and Pix in Brazil, eliminating merchant credit card fees.

key_trends.explanation: Using fiat-backed digital tokens (USDC, USDT) on public or permissioned blockchains for instant settlement.
key_trends.real_tech_example: Stripe allowing merchants to collect payments in USDC over Solana/Polygon networks, settling cross-border payments in seconds instead of 5 days via SWIFT.

key_trends.explanation: Using unique physical biometric identifiers linked to a tokenized bank account.
key_trends.real_tech_example: Amazon One palm-scanning payment terminals deployed at Whole Foods markets, allowing customers to pay by waving their hand over a infrared sensor.

key_trends.explanation: Automated software agents executing micro-transactions on behalf of users using programmatic smart wallets.
key_trends.real_tech_example: An Autonomous AI Travel Agent renting server GPUs or booking flight APIs per millisecond using x402 digital micro-payments.

topics.title: What is Single Sign-On (SSO)?
topics.overview: SSO is an authentication architecture that allows a user to authenticate once with a master Identity Provider and gain authorized access to multiple independent software systems.

key_term_definitions.authentication: Verifying WHO you are (e.g., checking password/biometrics).
key_term_definitions.authorization: Verifying WHAT permissions you have (e.g., checking if you are an admin).
key_term_definitions.jwt_json_web_token: A compact, cryptographically signed token format used to securely transmit claims between two parties.

core_components.identity_provider_idp: The central server that stores user passwords and validates logins (e.g., Google Identity, Okta, Auth0).
core_components.service_provider_sp: The application the user wants to use (e.g., Slack, Notion, Zoom).
core_components.trust_relationship: A setup where the Service Provider trusts identity assertions signed by the Identity Provider's public/private cryptographic keys.

real_tech_flow_example: 1. User opens Google Workspace/Slack and clicks 'Log in with Google'.
2. Slack (Service Provider) redirects user to accounts.google.com (Identity Provider).
3. User enters password and completes 2FA on Google's page.
4. Google generates an encrypted, digitally signed token (ID Token / JWT) asserting 'This is Alex, email alex@tech.com'.
5. Browser sends this token back to Slack.
6. Slack verifies Google's cryptographic signature using Google's public key, extracts Alex's profile, and logs Alex in without ever seeing his Google password.

topics.title: How to Store Passwords Safely in a Database?
topics.golden_rule: NEVER store plain-text passwords, and NEVER use plain, fast hash functions like MD5, SHA-1, or SHA-256.

key_term_definitions.hashing: A one-way cryptographic mathematical function that transforms an input string into a fixed-length string. It cannot be reversed.
key_term_definitions.salt: A unique, cryptographically random string added to a password before hashing to prevent rainbow table (precomputed hash table) attacks.
key_term_definitions.brute_force_attack: An attack where a hacker tries millions of password combinations per second using powerful GPUs.

step_by_step_security_blueprint.explanation: Use algorithms intentionally engineered to be CPU/Memory intensive, making brute-force GPU cracking impossibly slow.
step_by_step_security_blueprint.recommended_tech: Argon2id (Winner of Password Hashing Competition), bcrypt, or PBKDF2.

step_by_step_security_blueprint.step: Generate a Unique Salt per Password
step_by_step_security_blueprint.explanation: Generate a 16-byte random string for every user registration. Append this salt to the password before running the hash.
step_by_step_security_blueprint.real_tech_example: If two users have the password 'Password123', their stored hashes will look completely different due to unique salts.

step_by_step_security_blueprint.explanation: A secret key stored outside the database (e.g., in AWS Secrets Manager or an HSM).
step_by_step_security_blueprint.real_tech_example: Even if an attacker leaks the entire SQL database, they cannot crack passwords because they lack the pepper stored in AWS hardware.

topics.title: How Does HTTPS Work?
topics.overview: HTTPS secures web traffic by encrypting HTTP requests and responses using Transport Layer Security (TLS).

key_term_definitions.asymmetric_encryption: Uses two keys: a Public Key (to encrypt data) and a Private Key (to decrypt data). Slow, but secure for key exchanges.
key_term_definitions.symmetric_encryption: Uses a single shared key to both encrypt and decrypt data. Extremely fast.
key_term_definitions.certificate_authority_ca: A globally trusted entity (e.g., Let's Encrypt, DigiCert) that verifies domain ownership and issues digital certificates.

tls_handshake_flow_tech_example: 1. ClientHello: Chrome browser sends request to https://amazon.com with supported TLS cipher versions.
2. ServerHello: Amazon server returns its TLS Certificate containing Amazon's Public Key.
3. CA Verification: Chrome verifies Amazon's certificate against root security certificates built into Windows/macOS.
4. Key Exchange (Diffie-Hellman): Browser and Server perform mathematical calculations to securely generate a shared 'Session Key' over the unencrypted network.
5. Symmetric Session Active: All future credit card details and search queries are encrypted using this fast shared 'Session Key'.

topics.title: How to Learn Design Patterns Effectively?
topics.overview: Design patterns are generalized, reusable solutions to recurring code architecture problems.

key_term_definitions.code_smell: A surface-level symptom in software code that indicates a deeper architectural flaw (e.g., duplicate code, massive classes).
key_term_definitions.refactoring: Restructuring existing software code without changing its external behavior.

learning_roadmap.details:
1. Creational (How objects are instantiated)
2. Structural (How objects are composed)
3. Behavioral (How objects communicate).

learning_roadmap.phase: Focus on Real Problems, Not Syntax
learning_roadmap.details: Understand what problem the pattern solves rather than memorizing code templates.

anchor_patterns_real_world_tech.real_tech_example: Payment Gateways: Creating a `PaymentFactory` that returns a `StripeService` or `PayPalService` based on user location.
Pub/Sub Systems: Notification systems (e.g., when a YouTube creator uploads a video, subscribers receive emails, push notifications, and feed updates).
Uber Navigation: Switching route algorithms dynamically based on travel mode (DrivingStrategy, WalkingStrategy, TransitStrategy).

topics.title: Visual Decision Guide for Choosing the Right Database

key_term_definitions.schema: The structured blueprint defining how tables, columns, and data types are organized in a database.
key_term_definitions.horizontal_scaling: Adding more server nodes to distribute data load (Sharding).
key_term_definitions.vertical_scaling: Upgrading a single server with more RAM and CPU power.

tech_decision_flow.question: Do you need strict ACID compliance, complex multi-table joins, and structured schemas?
tech_decision_flow.real_tech_example: Bank account ledgers, E-commerce order processing systems.

tech_decision_flow.question: Are you dealing with dynamic, semi-structured JSON documents with high write volumes?
tech_decision_flow.real_tech_example: E-commerce product catalog with varying item attributes (shoes have size, phones have RAM specs).

tech_decision_flow.question: Do you need ultra-low latency sub-millisecond data reads for ephemeral data?
tech_decision_flow.real_tech_example: User login session storage, Leaderboards, Rate-limiting counters.

tech_decision_flow.question: Are you capturing massive high-frequency time-stamped write logs or IoT sensor data?
tech_decision_flow.real_tech_example: Uber GPS vehicle location tracking history, server telemetry metrics.

tech_decision_flow.question: Do you need to query complex multi-hop relationships between entities?
tech_decision_flow.real_tech_example: LinkedIn '1st/2nd/3rd degree connections' recommendation engine or Fraud detection rings.

topics.title: How to Generate Globally Unique IDs at Scale?
topics.overview: Generating billions of non-colliding, sortable unique primary key IDs in distributed systems without bottlenecking central database auto-increments.

key_term_definitions.collision: An unintended event where two different records are assigned the exact same ID.
key_term_definitions.b_tree_index: The default self-balancing tree data structure used by databases to search indexed primary keys rapidly.

tech_approaches.pros: Fully decentralized generation in application code. Zero central coordination required.
tech_approaches.cons: Completely random string destroys database B-Tree index performance due to random disk page writes.
tech_approaches.real_tech_example: Generating temporary file upload session tokens.

tech_approaches.structure: 1-bit Sign | 41-bits Timestamp | 10-bits Worker Machine ID | 12-bits Sequence Counter
tech_approaches.pros: Fits inside standard 64-bit integer index (BIGINT); time-sortable; generates up to 4,096 IDs per millisecond per machine.
tech_approaches.real_tech_example: Twitter/X generating IDs for every Tweet so that feed sorting is naturally time-ordered.

tech_approaches.pros: 128-bit string that is fully time-sortable and URL-safe.
tech_approaches.real_tech_example: Modern API resource IDs in platforms like Segment and Supabase.

topics.title: How Does Twitter Work (High-Level System Design)?
topics.overview: Twitter handles massive read-to-write asymmetry (approx. 100:1 read vs write ratio) and solves the 'Celebrity Fan-out Problem'.

key_term_definitions.fanout: The process of delivering a message posted by one user to the feeds of millions of followers.
key_term_definitions.cache: High-speed in-memory data store (like Redis) sitting in front of slow databases.

system_architecture.write_path: User posts tweet -> API Gateway -> Tweet Service -> Save to Primary Database -> Push Event to Apache Kafka Queue.

fanout_service_hybrid_model.normal_users_push_model: When a user with 200 followers tweets, the Fanout Service pushes that Tweet ID into the Redis timeline cache of all 200 followers immediately.
fanout_service_hybrid_model.celebrities_pull_model: When a celebrity with 80 million followers (e.g., Elon Musk) tweets, pushing to 80 million caches causes system overload. Instead, followers dynamically fetch celebrity tweets upon opening their app and merge them with their local timeline.

topics.title: What is the Difference Between Process and Thread?

key_term_definitions.process: An executing instance of a computer program with its own isolated memory space.
key_term_definitions.thread: The smallest unit of execution within a process (often called a lightweight process).
key_term_definitions.context_switch: The CPU stopping one process/thread and loading another. Expensive for processes, cheap for threads.

memory.process: Isolated memory address space. Cannot read another process's memory without explicit IPC (Inter-Process Communication).
memory.thread: Shares address space, memory heap, and open file handles with sister threads inside same parent process.

comparison_table.overhead: Creating a process is heavy and slow. Creating a thread is fast and lightweight.
comparison_table.crash_isolation: If Chrome Tab Process A crashes, Chrome Tab Process B stays open. If Thread A in a process corrupts memory, the entire process crashes.
comparison_table.real_tech_example: Chrome browser uses a separate Process per open tab for stability. Node.js is single-process multi-threaded internally via libuv.

topics.title: System Design: How to Design Google Docs?
topics.overview: A system supporting real-time concurrent text editing across millions of simultaneous connected users.

key_term_definitions.operational_transformation_ot: An algorithm that modifies indices of concurrent edit operations so both users reach the exact same state.
key_term_definitions.crdt: Conflict-free Replicated Data Type - a data structure that enables decentralized merging of edits without requiring a central server authority.

architectural_components.realtime_transport: WebSockets maintaining full-duplex persistent TCP connections between client browsers and collaboration backend servers.
architectural_components.conflict_resolution: Google Docs uses Operational Transformation (OT). If User A inserts 'X' at position 3, and User B deletes position 3 simultaneously, the OT server adjusts User B's operation offset.
architectural_components.storage_stack: PostgreSQL for document metadata & access controls; S3/GCS blob storage for historical snapshots; Cassandra for storing append-only character edit stream operations.

topics.title: Modern Application Deployment Strategies

key_term_definitions.downtime: Period when a application service is unavailable to users.
key_term_definitions.load_balancer: A device/software routing network traffic across a cluster of healthy servers.

strategies.name: Rolling Deployment
strategies.mechanism: Incrementally update 25% of backend server instances at a time behind a load balancer until 100% are updated.
strategies.real_tech_example: Kubernetes rolling update strategy for microservices.

strategies.name: Blue/Green Deployment
strategies.mechanism: Maintain two production environments: Blue (current live v1.0) and Green (new v2.0). Switch load balancer router instantly to Green.
strategies.real_tech_example: AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment URL swap. Allows instant rollback if v2.0 fails.

strategies.name: Canary Deployment
strategies.mechanism: Route 2% of live production traffic to v2.0. If error rates remain normal, gradually ramp up to 100%.
strategies.real_tech_example: Netflix rollout testing new video streaming algorithm changes on a small region before worldwide deployment.

topics.title: Flowchart Logic: How Slack Decides to Send a Notification
topics.overview: Slack avoids annoying users by evaluating context rules across multiple devices before triggering alerts.
step_by_step_flowchart_logic: 1. Event: User B posts a message mentioning User A (@Alex).
2. Check Desktop Client: Is User A active on Slack Desktop App with window in focus?
-> YES: Update UI badge counter silently. DO NOT send push notification. STOP.
3. Check DND Status: Is User A in Do-Not-Disturb mode or out of working hours?
4. Check Mobile Push: Is User A connected via active Mobile connection?
-> YES: Delay 25 seconds. If message remains unread, send Apple APNS / Google FCM Mobile Push Notification. STOP.
-> NO: Send Email Digest after 15 minutes.

topics.title: How Does Amazon Build and Operate Software?

key_term_definitions.ci_cd: Continuous Integration & Continuous Deployment - automated pipelines that build, test, and ship code changes to production.
key_term_definitions.post_mortem: A meeting and document reviewing a system failure to prevent reoccurrence.

core_operating_pillars.explanation: Autonomous product teams sized small enough (6-10 people) to be fed by two large pizzas. Each team owns one service end-to-end ('You build it, you run it').
Teams cannot share database tables. They must strictly communicate via exposed REST/gRPC APIs (The Bezos API Mandate).
Code builds move automatically through pipeline stages: Alpha -> Beta -> Gamma -> One small AWS Region (e.g., Ireland) -> Global Regions, with auto-rollback triggers if latency spikes.

topics.title: How to Design Secure Web API Access for Your Website?

key_term_definitions.rate_limiting: Restricting the number of API requests a client can make within a given time frame.
key_term_definitions.cors: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing - a browser security mechanism that restricts resources requested from another domain.

security_architecture_layers.protection: Place Web Application Firewall (AWS WAF / Cloudflare) at entry point to block SQL Injections, Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), and DDoS attacks.
Implement Token Bucket algorithm in Redis to enforce max 100 requests per minute per IP address.
Issue short-lived JWT Access Tokens (15 min expiry) along with HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite-restricted Refresh Cookies.

topics.title: How Do Microservices Collaborate and Interact?

key_term_definitions.synchronous: Client sends request and waits (blocked) for server response.
key_term_definitions.asynchronous: Client sends event to a message broker and moves on without waiting for processing to complete.

interaction_patterns.use_case: Order Checkout API needing immediate payment status response.
interaction_patterns.real_tech_example: Web App calling User Service via REST API to fetch user avatar.
Uber Trip Finished Event published to Kafka. Fraud Service, Invoice Service, and Driver Rating Service process event asynchronously without slowing down driver app.

topics.title: Virtualization (VMware) vs Containerization (Docker)

key_term_definitions.hypervisor: Software that creates and runs Virtual Machines by virtualizing physical server hardware (e.g., VMware ESXi).
key_term_definitions.namespaces_and_cgroups: Linux kernel features that isolate process view (Namespaces) and limit resource usage like CPU/RAM (Cgroups).

virtualization_vm.architecture: Virtualizes underlying Hardware. Each VM runs a full guest Operating System (Ubuntu/Windows).
virtualization_vm.real_tech_example: AWS EC2 virtual server instances running multi-tenant hardware workloads.

containerization_docker.architecture: Virtualizes the Operating System kernel. Containers share host Linux kernel.
containerization_docker.real_tech_example: Deploying hundreds of lightweight microservice containers onto a single Kubernetes worker node.

topics.title: Which Cloud Provider Should Be Used for Big Data Solutions?

cloud_providers_compared.strengths: Native home of Big Data tools (Spanner, MapReduce, Kubernetes were created at Google).
cloud_providers_compared.real_tech_example: Spotify using GCP BigQuery to run analytics on billions of user music streams daily.

cloud_providers_compared.strengths: Most extensive catalog of integrated big data tools and vendor integrations.
cloud_providers_compared.real_tech_example: Airbnb running data lakes on AWS S3 coupled with EMR processing clusters.

topics.title: How to Avoid Crawling Duplicate URLs at Google Scale?

key_term_definitions.bloom_filter: A space-efficient probabilistic data structure used to test whether an element is definitely NOT in a set or PROBABLY in a set.
key_term_definitions.web_crawler: Automated bot (like Googlebot) that scans and indexes web pages across the internet.

engineering_pipeline.details: Strip tracking params (e.g., `?utm_source=twitter`), convert hostnames to lowercase, remove session IDs and anchor tags (`#section1`).
Query massive in-memory Bloom Filter array with normalized URL string. If Bloom Filter says 'No', URL is guaranteed new; proceed to crawl.
Calculate locality-sensitive fingerprint hash of page HTML. If two pages with different URLs have 99% identical SimHash values, drop duplicate page from search index.

topics.title: Why is a Solid-State Drive (SSD) Fast?

key_term_definitions.seek_time: The time required for a traditional hard drive read head to physically move to the disk platter track location.
key_term_definitions.nvme: Non-Volatile Memory Express  -  a high-speed interface protocol designed specifically for SSDs running over PCIe lines.

architectural_advantages.explanation: HDD requires spinning magnetic disks and moving arm heads (taking 5-10ms seek time). SSDs read electrical charges directly from NAND cells in under 0.05ms.
SSD controller chips read and write data simultaneously across dozens of NAND flash chips in parallel.
Bypasses legacy SATA controller bottlenecks (600 MB/s max) using direct PCIe lines capable of 7000+ MB/s transfer speeds.

topics.title: Step-by-Step Incident Management: Handling a Large-Scale Outage

key_term_definitions.incident_commander_ic: The designated person leading and coordinating the technical response during a critical outage.
key_term_definitions.post_mortem: A blameless engineering review document analyzing failure root causes and detailing preventative action items.

step_by_step_incident_runbook: 1. Detection & Triage: Telemetry monitoring (Datadog/Grafana) detects HTTP 5xx error spikes -> Alerts PagerDuty -> Rotates on-call engineer -> Incident Commander opens war room channel.
2. Mitigate Immediately (Stop the Bleed): Rollback recent code deployments, hit kill-switch feature flags for heavy features (e.g., recommendation carousel), or add server instances.
3. Public Communication: Post updates to status.yourcompany.com every 15-30 minutes ('Investigating issue with checkout pipeline').
4. Root Cause Analysis (RCA): Analyze logs in OpenSearch/Kibana to isolate bad database query or memory leak.
5. Blameless Post-Mortem: Write 5-Whys document and create Jira tickets for permanent architectural fixes.

topics.title: AWS Lambda Behind the Scenes Architecture

key_term_definitions.serverless: A cloud execution model where cloud providers automatically manage machine allocation and scaling; you pay only for precise execution time.
key_term_definitions.cold_start: The initialization delay experienced when a serverless function is invoked for the first time or after sitting idle.

internal_architecture.firecracker_microvm: AWS developed Firecracker  -  an open-source, lightweight Virtual Machine monitor written in Rust that creates lightweight secure microVMs in 5 milliseconds.

cold_start_vs_warm_start.cold_start: Request hits API Gateway -> Lambda control plane provisions Firecracker microVM -> Downloads code zip from S3 -> Starts runtime (e.g., Python) -> Executes function. Latency: 200ms-1s.
cold_start_vs_warm_start.warm_start: Subsequent requests reuse existing initialized, running Firecracker microVM instance directly. Latency: 5ms.

topics.title: Evolution of HTTP Protocols: HTTP/1.0 to HTTP/3 (QUIC)
topics.overview: HTTP has evolved over decades to overcome latency, head-of-line blocking, and connection setup overhead across modern web application delivery networks.

key_term_definitions.head_of_line_blocking: A performance bottleneck where a delayed packet or request blocks all subsequent queued packets or requests from being processed.
key_term_definitions.multiplexing: Interleaving multiple request/response signals concurrently over a single underlying network connection.
key_term_definitions.tcp_handshake: The three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) required to establish a reliable connection before transmitting data over TCP.

version_comparison.key_features: Creates a new TCP connection for every single HTTP request/response cycle.
version_comparison.drawbacks: Severe connection latency overhead due to repeated TCP 3-way handshakes for every image, JS, and CSS file.
version_comparison.real_tech_example: Early 1990s static web pages rendering basic HTML files.

version_comparison.key_features: Introduced Persistent Connections (`Keep-Alive`) to reuse single TCP connection, and HTTP Pipelining.
version_comparison.drawbacks: Suffers from HTTP-level Head-Of-Line (HOL) blocking if a single request stalls at the head of the queue.
version_comparison.real_tech_example: Legacy web applications relying on domain sharding and image spriting to download resources faster.

version_comparison.key_features: Binary framing layer, full Request/Response Multiplexing over a single TCP connection, HPACK header compression, Server Push.
version_comparison.drawbacks: TCP-level Head-Of-Line blocking: if a single TCP packet is dropped, OS TCP stack holds back all multiplexed streams until packet retransmission.
version_comparison.real_tech_example: Modern single-page web applications (React/Angular) fetching dozens of API assets concurrently from CDNs.

version_comparison.key_features: Replaces TCP with QUIC protocol over UDP. Built-in TLS 1.3 security handshake, stream-independent multiplexing, Connection ID mobility.
version_comparison.drawbacks: Requires client/server hardware to handle higher UDP packet processing CPU load; some firewalls block UDP port 443.
version_comparison.real_tech_example: Google Search, YouTube, and Meta mobile apps switching cellular networks (WiFi to 5G) without dropping active video calls or web requests.

topics.title: How to Scale a Website to Support Millions of Concurrent Users?
topics.overview: Scaling a system requires systematically identifying bottlenecks and moving from a monolithic single-server setup to a horizontally partitioned, multi-region distributed system.

key_term_definitions.stateless_architecture: Designing backend app servers so they store no user session state in local server memory, allowing any server instance to handle any request.
key_term_definitions.database_sharding: Horizontal partitioning of database tables across multiple physical database server instances.

evolutionary_scaling_steps.components: App Server + Database running on a single AWS EC2 instance.
evolutionary_scaling_steps.bottleneck: Single point of failure; hard hardware limits on CPU/RAM.

evolutionary_scaling_steps.components: Add Application Load Balancer (ALB), scale out stateless App instances, separate Primary DB (Writes) from Read Replicas, add Redis Cache for hot data.
evolutionary_scaling_steps.real_tech_example: E-commerce platform serving 90% read traffic from Redis/Replicas while routing 10% checkout writes to Primary DB.

evolutionary_scaling_steps.components: Serve images, JS, CSS, and media directly through Cloudflare or AWS CloudFront edge locations globally.
evolutionary_scaling_steps.real_tech_example: Media platform like Netflix offloading 99% of media payload bandwidth from core backend servers to global edge nodes.

evolutionary_scaling_steps.components: Break monolith into microservices, shard relational databases by User_ID using Snowflake IDs, implement message queues (Kafka) for async processing.
evolutionary_scaling_steps.real_tech_example: Uber operating thousands of independent microservices backed by distributed NoSQL and sharded MySQL clusters.

topics.title: Essential DevOps & Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) Reading List

key_term_definitions.sre_site_reliability_engineering: A discipline that applies software engineering solutions to infrastructure operational and reliability problems.
key_term_definitions.infrastructure_as_code_iac: Managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable definition files (e.g., Terraform) rather than physical hardware configuration.

top_books.title: The Phoenix Project
top_books.authors: Gene Kim, Kevin Behr, George Spafford
top_books.core_focus: IT Operations, DevOps transformation, Agile manufacturing principles applied to software delivery.
top_books.key_takeaway: Introduces the Three Ways: Flow, Feedback, and Continual Learning.

top_books.authors: Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy

top_books.key_takeaway: Treat operations as a software problem; enforce Service Level Objectives (SLOs) to balance velocity vs stability.
